title: What is CORS and how do you configure it safely in ASP.NET Core?
description: Preflight requests, allowed origins vs credentials, middleware order, and what CORS does not protect against.

data.text: **Question:** What is CORS and how do you configure it safely in ASP.NET Core?

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a **browser-enforced** protocol that lets a server declare which other origins may read its responses. Without it, the browser's same-origin policy blocks your SPA on `app.example.com` from calling `api.example.com`. The server responds with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers; unsafe requests trigger a preflight `OPTIONS` check first. CORS constrains **browsers**, not other clients — a curl or Postman caller ignores it entirely, so authorization still has to be real.

**How the flow works:**
- Simple requests (GET/POST with safe headers) go out directly; the browser checks the response's `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`
- Everything else (custom headers, PUT/DELETE, `application/json` in some cases) triggers a **preflight OPTIONS** request — the server must approve method, headers, and origin before the real request is sent
- A missing or mismatched allow header surfaces as an opaque CORS error in the browser console — the request may have already reached the server

**Safe configuration rules:**
- List **explicit origins** — never `AllowAnyOrigin` for authenticated traffic
- `AllowCredentials` (cookies) is incompatible with wildcard origins — ASP.NET Core throws at runtime if you combine them
- Place `UseCors` before `UseAuthentication`/`UseAuthorization` so preflights resolve without challenging
- Use a named policy per client (SPA, mobile BFF) rather than one global allow-all
- CORS is not CSRF protection and not authentication: it does not verify *who* is calling
- Non-browser clients are unaffected — secure every endpoint on its own merits

data.title: Named CORS policy, safe defaults

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing CORS exists for the browser, not as an API security control
- Understanding preflight vs simple requests
- Practical rules: explicit origins, credentials+wildcard conflict, middleware order
- Clear separation from CSRF (CORS decides who may *read*; CSRF tokens guard unsafe *writes*)

items: AllowAnyOrigin on APIs with cookie or token auth — over-permissive by design
Putting UseCors after authentication, so preflight requests get 401 and the browser blocks everything
Thinking CORS stops attackers — curl, mobile apps, and server-side callers ignore it
Forgetting credentials: 'withOrigins but no AllowCredentials' means cookies are dropped and sessions break
Debugging CORS from the client only — the real answer is in the response headers the server sent
What happens during a preflight and which headers does the server return?
How is CORS different from CSRF protection?
A teammate says 'CORS is failing' — how do you verify from the server side?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CORS = browser-enforced origin allow-list with Access-Control-* headers
Unsafe requests are preceded by an OPTIONS preflight
Explicit origins + no wildcard with credentials; UseCors before auth
CORS constrains browsers only — authorization is still your job
data.takeaway: Configure CORS as a tight, per-client origin allow-list for your SPA — and never mistake it for authentication or attack protection.
